new_statements.translation: [p. VI] ' = after a vowel: accent; after a consonant: palatalization. [p. 81, 4.11.8 durative preterite] The stress lies on the ending -Ar, under negation on -mAz. [p. 83, 4.11.9 imperative] Stress: apart from emphatic stress, it lies on the stem with monosyllabic stems. Verbs that have a disyllabic stem have the stress on the second syllable. This also holds under negation. The 3rd plural has the stress on the last syllable. In the 2nd plural a contraction occurs after a stem-final vowel (see the examples above). [p. 89] Here the lengths, sometimes also the half-lengths and the accents, were taken into account.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tulu gives no general word-stress rule; stress is stated only inside two verb paradigms and is morphologically conditioned. In the durative preterite (aorist + past) the aorist suffix -Ar (negative -mAz) carries the stress and the following past/person endings do not (examples with the accent mark: diyä'rdın, itä'rdi, isteyä'rdi, bermä'sdi, gidä'rdilän). In the imperative the stress stays on the stem: on the only syllable of monosyllabic stems, on the second (final) stem syllable of disyllabic stems, also under negation; only the 3pl imperative (-sIlAn) has final stress. Emphatic stress is explicitly set aside. So the picture is stem-final/root stress in the imperative versus a stress-attracting aorist suffix elsewhere, i.e. placement set by the morphological category, not by a fixed position or by weight. The transcription key (p. VI) shows that an apostrophe after a vowel marks the accent, so the accented tokens in the wordlist and text are usable data (e.g. ga'ra 'schwarz' W558, ga'rin 'Bauch' W51 on p. 12 carry initial accent), but the book makes no statement about nominal stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Emphatic stress is excepted ('Abgesehen von der emphatischen Betonung'); the 3pl imperative has final stress unlike the other persons; in the 2pl imperative a vowel-final stem contracts with the ending. Under negation the stress falls on -mAz in the durative preterite and stays on the stem in the imperative.
new_statements.identity_note: Tulu 1989 describes the speech of the village Kalāt (Kalāt-e Esfarāyen, ca. 37.14 N / 57.20 E, 100 inhabitants, 25 km NW of Esfarāyen toward Bojnurd), recorded on 11 October 1973 during G. Doerfer's Khorasan expedition from one bakhshi (folk singer): a 714-word standard list, a grammatical questionnaire and the sung/spoken Aşıq-Kärä narrative (p. VII). Within Khorasan Turkic the Kalāt variety belongs to the NW dialect together with Bojnurdi (sec. 1.3, p. 12). The stress statements are drawn from that single speaker's material, largely sung or allegro text (p. 89), which is why Tulu sets emphatic stress aside and notes reductions.
